title: Of recompenses of honour
paragraphs: Those who write the life of Augustus Caesar note this point about his military discipline: he was wonderfully generous in giving material gifts to men of merit, but extremely sparing of the true recompenses of honour — even though his own uncle had granted him all the military honours before he had ever been in the field. It was a clever invention, adopted in most of the world's governments, to set up certain empty, intrinsically valueless distinctions to honour and reward virtue: crowns of laurel, oak, and myrtle; a particular cut of garment; the privilege of riding in a coach inside the city, or at night by torchlight; a special seat in public assemblies; the prerogative of certain additional names and titles; certain marks on a coat of arms; and the like. Their use, according to the temper of different nations, has varied, and they are still in use today.

We in France, like several of our neighbours, have orders of knighthood instituted specifically for this purpose. It is, in truth, a very good and useful custom to find some acknowledgement for the worth of rare and excellent men, and to satisfy them with rewards that cost neither prince nor people anything. And the fact, established by long experience and which we ourselves once observed, that men of quality have always been more jealous of such honours than of rewards involving gain and profit, has very good ground and reason behind it. If you mix in with the reward — which ought to be purely an honour — other goods and money on top, the mixture, instead of raising its esteem, debases and cheapens it. The Order of Saint Michael, which was long held in such repute among us, had no greater asset than this: it carried no other benefit attached to it. The result was that, formerly, there was no office or title which the gentry sought with such eagerness and affection as that one; no rank carried more respect and grandeur. Valour and worth were more eagerly drawn to, more ambitiously aimed at, a recompense purely their own — glorious rather than profitable. For other gifts have less dignity in use, because they are handed out on all sorts of occasions: with money you pay the wages of a servant, the speed of a courier, dancing, vaulting, talking, and the meanest services we receive; you even reward vices with it — flattery, treachery, pimping. No wonder, then, that virtue is less eager for, less ready to accept, this common kind of payment than one that is proper and peculiar to her, noble and generous through and through. Augustus had good reason to be more sparing with this than with material gifts, since honour is a privilege whose principal essence comes from its rarity; and virtue itself works the same way:
"Cui malus est nemo, quis bonus esse potest?"
["Where no one is bad, who can be good?" — Martial, xii. 82.]

We do not mean it as a compliment when we say that someone is careful in the education of his children, because it is a common act, however right and well done; any more than we praise a great tree where the whole forest is the same. I doubt any citizen of Sparta took much pride in his courage, since it was the universal virtue of the whole nation; or in his honesty and his contempt for riches. No recompense fits a virtue, however great, once it has become routine; and I am not sure that we can even call a thing great when it is common.

Since, then, these rewards of honour have no value or esteem beyond the fact that few people enjoy them, you only have to be generous with them to bring them down to nothing. And although there may now be more men deserving of our order than there used to be, its estimation still ought not to be lowered, nor its honour cheapened; in fact, it may easily turn out that more do deserve it, since there is no virtue that spreads as quickly as military valour. There is another virtue — the true, perfect, philosophical kind, of which I am not speaking, and the name of which I am only using in its common sense — much greater and fuller than this one: a steadiness and firmness of soul that despises all kinds of adverse accidents equally, even, uniform, and constant, of which the virtue we are discussing is only one little ray. Habit, education, example, and custom can do everything towards establishing the kind I am talking about, and can easily make it common, as the experience of our civil wars makes plain enough. Whoever could at this moment unite us all, Catholic and Huguenot, into one body and set us on some bold common enterprise would soon make our old military reputation flourish again. It is quite certain that in former times the reward of this order had its eye not only on valour but on something further: it never went to a brave soldier as such, but to a great captain; the science of obeying was not thought to deserve so honourable a prize. There was a more comprehensive military skill required for it, taking in most and the greatest qualities of a soldier:
"Neque enim eaedem militares et imperatoriae artes sunt,"
["For the arts of the soldier and of the general are not the same." — Livy, xxv. 19.]

— as well as a station in life suitable to such a dignity. But, I say, even if more men were worthy of it than formerly, it still ought not to be more freely handed out. Better to err in not giving it to people who would have deserved it than to lose for good, as we have recently done, the fruit of so useful an invention. No man of spirit will deign to take pride in something he holds in common with many; and those of our own day who have least deserved this recompense are the loudest in pretending to disdain it, so as to rank themselves with those whose particular right has been wronged by the unworthy giving away of the distinction.

Now, to think that by wiping out and abolishing this order we can suddenly create and bring into credit another like it, is not a proper undertaking for so undisciplined and sick a time as ours. The new one will from the start run into the same problems that have ruined the old. The rules for handing out this new order would need to be tightly drawn and hedged in by strict limits, in order to give it authority — and this turbulent age cannot bear such a curb. Besides, before any new one can come into repute, the memory of the first, and of the contempt into which it has fallen, must first be buried in oblivion.

This is a natural enough place to bring in some discussion of valour, and how this virtue differs from others; but since Plutarch has handled the subject so often, I would only be giving myself extra work by repeating what he has said. It is, however, worth noting that our nation puts valour, vaillance, at the top of all the virtues, as the word itself shows, deriving from valeur. In our usage, when we say a man of high worth or a good man in our court style, it means a valiant man, after the Roman fashion; for the general term for virtue with them comes from vis, force. The proper, sole, and essential profession of the French nobility is arms; and it is likely that the first virtue which showed itself among men and gave some an advantage over others was the one by which the strongest and bravest mastered the weaker and gained particular authority and reputation — hence its honoured name; or else these nations, being very warlike, gave first place to the virtue they were most familiar with. In just the same way, our own anxious obsession with the chastity of women makes the phrase a good woman, a woman of worth, a woman of honour and virtue mean nothing more than a chaste woman, as if, to bind them to that one duty, we were content to ignore all the rest and gave them free rein in all other faults, provided they avoided that one of incontinence.
